hints: Look carefully at the two particles involved, a neutral but polar water molecule and a fully charged metal cation.
Remember water has a partial negative charge on oxygen, $δ-$, which will be attracted to the positive $+$ charge of the cation.
Think about the name given to an attraction between a full ion and a polar molecule with opposite partial charges.
walkthrough:
**Identify the two particles**

Think side by side with me. Water, $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, is a neutral molecule but it is polar. Oxygen pulls electrons more strongly, so we write it as $\text{O}^{\delta-}-\text{H}^{\delta+}$.

A metal cation, for example $\text{Na}^+$ or $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, is a full positive ion with a complete $+$ or $2+$ charge.

**Match the attraction to its name**

A full ion attracting a partial charge on a polar molecule has a special name in chemistry.

It is not dipole-dipole, because that is between two neutral polar molecules. It is not a full ionic bond, because no electrons are transferred to water.

**See hydration in action**

In solution the $\delta-$ oxygen end of several water molecules points in toward the cation and surrounds it. This forms the hydrated ion, e.g. $[\text{Na}(\text{H}_2\text{O})_6]^{+}$.

This stabilising attraction between ion and polar solvent is called ion-dipole interaction.

options.A: Dipole-dipole interactions occur between two neutral polar molecules, such as between two $\text{HCl}$ molecules. Here one particle is a full ion, not a dipole, so this name is too weak and incorrect.
options.B: Hydrogen bonds occur between water molecules themselves, where $\text{H}^{\delta+}$ is attracted to a lone pair on O, N or F. The attraction of water to a metal cation does not involve H-bond donation to the metal, so this is a common confusion.
options.C: Correct and well done. The full positive charge of the cation attracts the $\delta-$ oxygen end of the polar water molecule. This ion to dipole attraction hydrates the cation and releases hydration enthalpy.
options.D: Ionic bonds are strong electrostatic attractions within a solid lattice between oppositely charged ions, with electron transfer. In solution the cation is surrounded by neutral water molecules, not bonded ionically to them.
